content: Travel nursing emerged as a response to the nursing shortage, where nurses are relocated to fill short-term positions. The current critical shortage of nurses in the United States has significantly increased the demand for these roles. Hospitals and recruitment agencies are offering various incentives to attract qualified registered nurses (RNs), licensed practical nurses (LPNs), licensed vocational nurses (LVNs), and allied health professionals. These incentives include relocation assistance, furnished housing, stipends, and bonuses. Travel Nursing Overview Many nurses are drawn to travel nursing for three primary reasons: the opportunity to work in diverse locations, access to free benefits, and the potential for higher salaries with bonuses. Nurses only need to apply once with a travel nursing company, which allows them to apply for multiple positions simultaneously without repeatedly filling out their information. Additionally, travel nurses can choose to remain in their current residence and receive a subsidy for their mortgage or rent if they prefer not to relocate. The travel nursing process is typically outlined in five steps, as described on MedStaff's About Travel Nursing page, to assist nurses unfamiliar with this career path. Clinical Requirements To become a travel nurse, the standard requirement is at least one year of clinical experience in a specific specialty and licensure in the state of employment. Licensure is often granted through reciprocity with the nurse's home state's board of nursing. While one year of experience is the minimum, it is strongly recommended to have two or more years of experience before pursuing travel nursing. Travel nurses often receive minimal orientation at their assignment hospital, typically lasting one or two days, or in some cases, no orientation at all. This should be clarified during the interview and explicitly written into the contract. Assignment hospitals expect travel nurses to be highly experienced and proficient in their specialty. If a nurse's home state is part of the Nurse Licensure Compact (NLC), they can work in any compact state using their home state license. However, the nurse must hold an RN or LPN license in good standing in their resident compact state. Currently, 21 states participate in the NLC, with two additional states pending implementation. Travel Nursing Assignments Travel nurses usually work under short-term contracts, typically ranging from 4 to 13 weeks. Contracts outside the United States can last 1 to 2 years. At the end of a contract, hospitals may offer an extension or even a permanent position. Assignment Housing Travel nursing companies generally provide a one-bedroom furnished apartment, though other housing arrangements can be made. Utilities such as electricity, water, and trash are often included within certain limits. Additional services like telephone, cable TV, and internet may also be provided. Housing typically includes basic furnishings and may feature appliances such as a washer, dryer, dishwasher, and microwave. Many companies also supply housewares, including pots, dishes, utensils, and linens. Housing is usually arranged by the travel nursing agency in the company's name, though some agencies allow nurses to participate in the housing search and selection process. In certain regions, securing reasonable housing can be more challenging. Most agencies offer a housing stipend if the nurse opts to arrange housing independently. Some companies require nurses to take the housing stipend and set up housing in their own name, claiming it may be more financially beneficial, though this is not always accurate. If the nurse does not have a permanent tax home, the housing stipend or provided housing will be taxed as part of their pay. Assignment Reimbursements Travel agencies typically provide a travel allowance, which may or may not cover all travel expenses. Some agencies offer healthcare insurance or reimbursement for insurance obtained elsewhere, the ability to contribute to 401(k) accounts (sometimes with matching funds), licensure reimbursement, referral bonuses for recruiting other travelers, and loyalty reward programs. Increasingly, companies are adding benefits such as vacation and sick days, stock investment options, and continuing education reimbursements. Salary and Benefits Salaries for travel nurses vary widely depending on factors such as location, hospital or unit needs, perceived staffing shortages, and the nurse's negotiation skills. Generally, southern regions of the United States pay less than northern or western regions. Areas with high housing costs can also influence salary ranges. Travel nurses may benefit from tax advantages, commonly referred to as Tax Advantage or Per Diem pay, if they maintain a permanent tax home while working and living away from that home. Tax-free reimbursements can cover meals, incidentals, and lodging. Some companies only offer tax-free lodging reimbursements, while others provide both. A permanent tax home is defined as a dwelling that the nurse lives in, maintains, and returns to between assignments. Tax-free money is a complex subject, and many travel companies lack a thorough understanding of the tax implications for nurses. Some companies encourage nurses who do not qualify to accept tax-free money, which can put them at risk during an IRS audit. It is strongly recommended to consult a travel tax expert before accepting tax-free money. Considerations There are additional costs associated with being a travel nurse, such as licensing fees and travel expenses. These costs are reimbursed to varying degrees depending on the company, recruiter, and the nurse's negotiation skills. While many nurses view travel nursing as a way to achieve financial stability and explore new places, it can become a challenging experience if the nurse is not adequately prepared and informed. To succeed as a travel nurse, it is essential to practice sound financial planning, maintain a flexible outlook, know which companies and recruiters to work with, ask the right questions, and negotiate effectively. The best advice on avoiding pitfalls and finding solutions often comes from traveler-produced websites, blogs, and forums. The number of LVN/LPN travel nurses is currently unknown.
